LESSON 86 OF 106·Offensive Thinking and Safe Testing

Bug Bounty and Responsible Disclosure

How a disclosure programme works: the floor that a policy sets, what a bounty adds, the report format as a two-sided contract, and why the last step is the only one that changes anything public.

Applied Foundation14 min
Why this matters

A bug bounty pays for findings that would otherwise be a gamble. Responsible disclosure is the same activity without the payment. Both are legitimate, and both depend entirely on a defined safe harbour.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

  1. Source: A programme states what is in scope, what is out of scope, and what is prohibited, usually including denial of service and social engineering of staff.

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.
  2. Weakness: Check the scope list before testing anything, and treat anything not named as excluded.
  3. Impact: The component trusts unverified data, crossing a confidentiality or integrity boundary.
01 Untrusted Input

02 Server Policy Gate

03 Verified Operation
  1. Verification: Publish a programme or at least a security contact and a safe harbour, even if you do not pay bounties.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A programme states what is in scope, what is out of scope, and what is prohibited, usually including denial of service and social engineering of staff.
  • Safe harbour is the promise that good-faith research will not be pursued, and without it a researcher is gambling.
  • Severity is set by the programme, usually based on impact rather than on how clever the technique was.
  • A report needs reproduction steps, impact, and a suggested remediation, which is what makes it actionable.
  • Duplicates and out-of-scope submissions are common, so expectations should be set before the work starts.

The background

  • Researchers found vulnerabilities first and had no formal route, so disclosure was public and often disruptive.
  • Early programmes at large vendors created both a payment model and a written safe harbour.
  • Platforms aggregated many programmes, which made it possible to hunt across a wide scope as routine work.
  • Programmes matured to publish response times and scope, which is what makes them usable by outsiders.

Real-world examples

  • A researcher who tests beyond the stated scope, or causes an outage, can lose the safe harbour protection and face legal action.
  • A report without demonstrated impact is often triaged low, even when the underlying bug is real.
  • A programme that never responds teaches researchers to publish instead, which is worse for everyone.

What to look for

  • Check the scope list before testing anything, and treat anything not named as excluded.
  • Check the prohibited actions, which usually include denial of service and automated scanning outside a rate limit.
  • Check whether the programme has an explicit safe harbour and a disclosed response time.
  • Check how severity is determined, so you know what outcome to aim for.

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Publish a programme or at least a security contact and a safe harbour, even if you do not pay bounties.
  • State scope and exclusions explicitly, since ambiguity is what causes most disputes.
  • Commit to a response time, and meet it, because silence is what pushes researchers to publish.
  • Run a triage process that separates impact from novelty, so researchers optimise for the right thing.
  • Credit reporters, which is a strong incentive for good behaviour and costs very little.
